studies.title: What Takes All Your Attention
studies.meaning: The two things named are not vices. Wealth and children are the ordinary goods of a life, and the ayah does not ask anyone to give them up; it names what they can do, which is occupy the attention completely. The verb is about being amused or absorbed rather than being corrupted. The verdict at the end is commercial: whoever lets that happen is not called wicked but is called a loser, someone whose accounts came out short.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of a short surah about people who said one thing publicly and another in private. The ayat before quote them refusing to spend and threatening to expel others from Medina. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Its placement matters: after a portrait of people ruined by calculation, the same warning is turned on the believers, and the possessions named are ordinary ones.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind amusement and diversion. It describes attention pulled elsewhere rather than turned against something, so the failure named is passive and requires no decision to occur.
The word covers calling to mind, saying aloud and keeping in view. It is not restricted to a formula, which is why the ayah can treat an entire mode of attention as the thing at risk.

keyTerms.gloss: the losers, those at a loss
keyTerms.note: A trading word for someone whose capital has been reduced. It implies a transaction that took place and went badly, not a person who never traded, which is a sharper description than simple failure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was countable: palms, camels, sacks of dates, and a man knew his holdings to the tree. Sons were the other kind of wealth, since a household with grown sons could defend itself, work its land and marry into better families. Both were what you worked for your whole life. The ayah names the two things everyone was legitimately busy with and says they can take the whole of you.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of wealth and children turns up repeatedly in the Quran and is treated in three different ways: as an adornment of this life, as a test, and here as a distraction. None of the three calls them bad. The consistency of the pairing suggests a settled assessment: the two greatest goods available to a person are also the two greatest occupiers of attention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The danger identified is not a rival object of worship but a full diary. That is a different kind of warning, and it applies to people whose lives are entirely legitimate. It also implies that remembrance is not something added on top of a life but something a life can crowd out, which makes attention the scarce resource rather than time or money. The consequence is stated as loss rather than as guilt.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the scene this warning is designed to prevent, a person asking for more time at the end.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your attention actually went yesterday, not where your time went. They are different measurements. Then pick the hour when your mind is most fully taken up by work or by family and put ten seconds of remembrance inside it, on purpose, without leaving the room. The ayah is about attention, so the fix has to happen there.
